lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Antisthenes, Crates — we have nothing on. So why don’t we walk straight over to the entrance and watch the new arrivals coming down: what sort they are, and what each of them does?

lines.speaker: Antisthenes
lines.text: Let’s go, Diogenes. It should be a pleasant spectacle: some of them crying, some actually begging to be let go, some barely coming down at all, with Hermes shoving them by the neck while they still dig in their heels and brace themselves flat on their backs. Pointlessly, of course.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: I can tell you what I saw when I was coming down the road myself.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Tell us, Crates. You look as if you saw something extremely funny.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: There were plenty of others coming down with us; among them three distinguished specimens: Ismenodorus, our rich man; Arsaces, the satrap of Media; and Oroetes the Armenian.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Ismenodorus had been murdered by bandits near Cithaeron — on his way to Eleusis, I think. He kept groaning, clutching the wound with both hands, calling for the little children he had left behind, still babies, and blaming himself for his daring: crossing Cithaeron and passing through the utterly deserted country around Eleutherae, with the wars on, and bringing only two servants with him — while carrying five gold bowls and four cups.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Arsaces, meanwhile — already an old man, and, by Zeus, not unimpressive to look at — was taking it in a very barbarian spirit. He was furious at having to walk, and demanded that his horse be brought to him. The horse had died with him, you see: both of them skewered by a single thrust from a Thracian peltast in the skirmish by the Araxes against the Cappadocian.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Arsaces said he had charged ahead, far out in front of the rest. The Thracian stood his ground, ducked under his little shield, knocked aside Arsaces’ lance, and then, planting his sarissa, ran both him and the horse through.

lines.speaker: Antisthenes
lines.text: How is that possible, Crates — with one thrust?

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Very easily, Antisthenes. Arsaces came charging with a lance sticking out in front of him, twenty cubits long if it was an inch. The Thracian parried the attack with his shield; the point went past him. Then he dropped to one knee and received the charge on his sarissa.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: The horse, all rage and momentum, impaled itself under the breast. Arsaces was driven clean through from the groin to just under the buttock. You see how it happened: not really the man’s work so much as the horse’s. Still, Arsaces was offended at being treated like everyone else, and insisted on entering as a cavalryman.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Oroetes was even better. His feet were so tender he could not even stand on the ground, let alone walk. Medes all suffer from this, apparently: the moment they get off their horses they tiptoe along as if stepping on thorns.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: So when he threw himself down and lay there, refusing by any method whatever to get up, excellent Hermes picked him up and carried him all the way to the ferry. I laughed.

lines.speaker: Antisthenes
lines.text: When I came down, I did not mix with the others either. I left them howling, ran ahead to the ferry, and secured a place in advance, so I could have a comfortable crossing. During the voyage they wept and were seasick. I enjoyed myself very much.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: You two, Crates and Antisthenes, had fellow-travellers of that sort. Mine were Blepsias the moneylender from Pisa, Lampis the Acarnanian mercenary captain, and Damis the rich Corinthian.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Damis had died from poison administered by his son. Lampis had cut his own throat over Myrtium the courtesan. Blepsias, poor devil, was said to have shrivelled up from starvation — and he certainly looked it: remarkably pale, and reduced to the exact minimum thickness.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Though I knew perfectly well, I questioned them on how they had died. Damis blamed his son, so I said, ‘You did not exactly suffer injustice at his hands: not if you had a thousand talents, were living in luxury yourself at ninety years old, and gave an eighteen-year-old boy four obols.’

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Then to the Acarnanian — he was groaning too, and cursing Myrtium — I said, ‘Why blame Love, when you ought to blame yourself? You never ran from the enemy; you fought at the front like a man who enjoyed danger. And then brave fellow that you are, you were captured by some little girl’s fake tears and sighs.’

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Blepsias had got there first and accused himself, at length, of stupidity: how he had hoarded his money for heirs no relation to him, the fool, imagining he would live forever. In any case, their groaning supplied me with no ordinary amusement.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: But here we are at the mouth now. We should look out and inspect the people arriving from a distance. Well, well. A large and varied lot — and all crying, except these newborns and infants. But even the very old are lamenting. What is this? Does life have them under some love-charm?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: I want to question this extremely elderly one. Why are you crying, dying at your age? Why so indignant, my good man — arriving here old? Surely you were some kind of king?

lines.speaker: Old Pauper
lines.text: Not at all.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: A satrap, then?

lines.speaker: Old Pauper
lines.text: Not that either.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Were you rich, then? Are you distressed because you died leaving a great deal of luxury behind?

lines.speaker: Old Pauper
lines.text: Nothing like that. I was about ninety. I made a living with a reed and a fishing-line, was poor to the point of excess, childless besides, lame, and with very dim sight.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And being like that, you still wanted to live?

lines.speaker: Old Pauper
lines.text: Yes. The light was sweet. Being dead is terrible, and to be avoided.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: You’re raving, old man. You’re acting like a boy in the face of necessity — and at your age, practically the ferryman’s contemporary. What can anyone say about the young, if people as old as this are so in love with life? Men who ought to be chasing death as medicine for the troubles of old age.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Come on, let’s go, before someone suspects us of planning an escape, seeing us loitering around the entrance.
